newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka grounds air force AN-32s after crash.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka grounds air force AN-32s after crash.

text.p: Sri Lanka's air force has temporarily grounded its remaining four Russian-made Antonov-32 transport planes after one crashed during take-off last week, a top air force official said on Wednesday.
"The AN-32s will be on ground for two or three days at the maximum," said deputy air force chief Air Vice Marshal Anslem Peiris.
"It is a temporary precaution we have taken until investigations into last Friday's crash are completed," Peiris told Reuters
But he said the temporary grounding would not affect the transporation of troops and material to the northern front where the military is battling separatist Tamil rebels.

The AN-32 plane with 59 people, including four crew, on board veered off the runway during take-off last Friday and crashed into a marshy patch at Ratmalana airbase, 11 km (seven miles) south of Colombo.

The airplane was bound for Palaly, a key northern base used by the military to battle the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), which is fighting for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in the island's north and east.
Three servicemen were killed and 36 were injured in the crash, the third involving an AN-32 during the past two years.

Sri Lanka's tiny air force has lost seven transport planes, one transport helicopter, two fighter aircraft and one unmanned drone since the war resumed in April 1995 after a 100-day truce was broken by the LTTE.
But Peiris said it was not a setback to the military operation against the LTTE.
"We don't foresee any major problems. We have enough planes to see us through."

He said the air force had two British-built Avros, nine Chinese-built Y-12 aircraft and 11 Russian-made MI-17 transport helicopters that can be used to ferry troops and supplies to key northern bases till the AN-32's are pushed back into service.

The air force lost its first Antonov in September 1995 when it crashed into the sea near Colombo with 75 servicemen on board. Bad weather and suspected instrument failure was given as the possible cause of the crash.
In November that year, a second AN-32 disappeared from radar over the northern seas with 68 servicemen aboard. It was believed to have been shot down by the rebels.
